sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in St. John's homes
sections.html:
Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical St. John's house dates from 1971–1980, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. That's about 16% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the St. John's area, 58% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, about 7% with a heat pump, about 7% with a boiler and radiators and about 6% with a forced-air furnace; electricity is the main heating energy for 65% of households and oil for 12% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

blower-door-test.lede: A blower door test measures how leaky a house is and shows where the leaks are. In St. John's, with about 4,578 heating degree-days a year, every leak runs up the heating bill for most of the year.

sections.h2: Why air leakage matters in St. John's
sections.html:
St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. That's about 16% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover.

Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses usually test leakier than newer ones, and an EnerGuide report compares your result with homes of the same era, so you can see whether your house is typical or a problem.

sections.h2: After you seal: two checks
sections.html:
• Combustion safety. In the St. John's area, the main heating energy is oil for 12% of households. A tighter house changes how fuel-burning appliances vent, so the spillage check should be repeated after serious air sealing. Combustion safety testing in St. John's
  • Radon. Sealing shifts the pressure balance between the house and the soil. Health Canada's 2012 survey found 4% of 100 homes tested in the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority health region above the guideline. In the City of St. John's free test-kit program, about 345 kits went out in November 2024 and 278 homes completed testing over the winter; about one in ten of them were above Health Canada's 200 Bq/m³ guideline. The participants were volunteers, so it isn't a random survey. Test before and after big air-sealing jobs. Radon testing in St. John's

sections.h2: What it costs in St. John's
sections.html: A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. There's no province-wide price; takeCHARGE lists the service organizations working in the province without prices.

sections.h2: How the test works
sections.html:
• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.h1: Heat loss calculations in St. John's
heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in St. John's: CSA F280-12 heat pump sizing for −12.8°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280-12 room-by-room heat loss calculation for St. John's homes, sized to the local −12.8°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −12.8°C for St. John's, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in St. John's
sections.html:
−12.8°C is the 12th-mildest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −12.8°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the St. John's area, 58% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, about 7% with a heat pump, about 7% with a boiler and radiators and about 6% with a forced-air furnace; electricity is the main heating energy for 65% of households and oil for 12% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

sections.h2: What CSA F280-12 asks for
sections.html: The National Building Code 2020 requires the heating capacity for a house to be worked out with CSA F280, and its list of referenced documents names the 2012 edition, CSA F280-12. Provincial codes can name their own edition and climate values, so ask your designer which ones the calculation uses.

sections.h2: Why skipping it costs money
sections.html: Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

sections.h2: What it costs
sections.html: About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

radon-testing.h1: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in St. John's
radon-testing.title: Radon testing in St. John's: long-term monitoring, kits and mitigation
radon-testing.description: Radon in St. John's: Health Canada survey results for the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority region (4% above the guideline), how to run a 91-day long-term test, digital monitors versus alpha-track kits, and mitigation by C-NRPP professionals ($2,000–$3,000).
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 4% of homes tested in the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority health region were above the guideline, and only a long-term test tells you about your own house.

sections.h2: Radon in St. John's
sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 4% of 100 homes tested in the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority health region above the guideline. In the City of St. John's free test-kit program, about 345 kits went out in November 2024 and 278 homes completed testing over the winter; about one in ten of them were above Health Canada's 200 Bq/m³ guideline. The participants were volunteers, so it isn't a random survey.

No survey can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely. Testing is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Long-term monitoring: how to test properly
sections.html:
Health Canada's measurement guide asks for a long-term test with at least 91 days in the heating season, when closed windows and the stack effect make readings higher, so the result is a conservative estimate of the yearly average. It recommends testing for 3 to 12 months. Our radon testing guide walks through each step.

Place the detector on the lowest level where someone spends more than four hours a day, at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls, and at least 1 m from vents, windows and doors; avoid kitchens, laundry rooms and bathrooms. The choice of device:

  • Alpha track detectors record radon's alpha particles on a plastic film; you mail them to a lab when the test ends. A long-term kit costs about $30–$80 including the lab fee (Windsor-Essex County Health Unit).
  • Electret ion chambers lose charge as radon ionizes the air inside; a lab reads the voltage drop.
  • Digital (electronic) monitors read continuously and show results on a screen or an app, and cost more (Lung Saskatchewan sells one for $189). For a long-term test, Health Canada says to use one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing, and it still has to run at least three months.
  • Continuous monitoring after mitigation: a digital monitor left running lets you watch for changes between the follow-up long-term tests Health Canada recommends.

sections.h2: Kits and professionals in St. John's
sections.html:
• There's no provincial kit program; several NL public libraries lend radon monitors.
  • The City of St. John's has run free radon kit programs for residents, including about 250 kits in its November 2025 round.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your St. John's postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: If your level is high: mitigation
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends fixing levels above 200 Bq/m³ within a year, and sooner the higher the level. The usual fix is a sub-slab depressurization system (a sealed pipe through the floor and a fan venting outside), which Health Canada says costs about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour and cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Hire a professional certified for mitigation under C-NRPP. After a system goes in:

  • A C-NRPP professional runs a short test starting at least 24 hours after the fan is turned on.
  • A long-term three-month test follows in the next fall or winter, done by a company other than the installer.
  • With an active system, Health Canada recommends a long-term test within two years of activation and every five years after that, and again after renovations.
  • Check the system's pressure gauge (manometer) regularly and never switch the fan off. It costs about $50 to $75 a year to run; a replacement fan is $200 to $300.

sections.h2: Rules and help in Newfoundland and Labrador
sections.html:
• Newfoundland and Labrador leaves building rules for new houses to municipal by-laws, so radon measures in new homes depend on the municipality.
  • The Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in St. John's?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 4% of 100 homes tested in the Eastern Regional Integrated Health Authority health region above the guideline. In the City of St. John's free test-kit program, about 345 kits went out in November 2024 and 278 homes completed testing over the winter; about one in ten of them were above Health Canada's 200 Bq/m³ guideline. The participants were volunteers, so it isn't a random survey. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least 91 days, in the heating season. Health Canada recommends 3 to 12 months; short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in St. John's?
faq.a: There's no provincial kit program; several NL public libraries lend radon monitors. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits, for about $30–$80 including the lab fee.

faq.q: Digital radon monitor or alpha-track kit?
faq.a: An alpha-track kit is the cheaper long-term test: it sits for three months or more and goes to a lab. A digital monitor shows readings as it goes and can keep running after mitigation; for a long-term result, use one that has passed C-NRPP testing and run it for at least three months.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Health Canada puts a sub-slab depressurization system at about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour, plus about $50 to $75 a year to run the fan. Hire a C-NRPP-certified mitigation professional.

faq.q: Should I keep monitoring after mitigation?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test in the following heating season, another within two years of activation, and one every five years after that. A digital monitor running in between shows if anything changes.

mold-testing.description: Mould inspection and indoor air quality testing in St. John's: when mold sampling is worth it, why damp coastal winters cause condensation, the CMHC and Health Canada size rules for cleanup, and when to hire a remediation contractor.
mold-testing.lede: Mould sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mould problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure. Here's how to inspect a home in St. John's, when air quality testing helps, and how much cleanup you can safely do yourself.

glance.sub: or if it keeps coming back

sections.h2: Why mould shows up in St. John's homes
sections.html:
St. John's gets about 4,578 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −12.8°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for St-John's International. Mild, wet winters keep materials damp, so poorly vented bathrooms, basements and crawlspaces are the usual suspects.

Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

sections.h2: Mould inspection: when sampling is worth it
sections.html:
Start by looking and smelling: stains, discoloured patches, peeling paint and a musty odour, especially in basements, bathrooms, window frames and closets on outside walls. Health Canada says measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually unnecessary.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Air or surface sampling helps in three cases:

  • You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

sections.h2: Cleanup and remediation: the size rules
sections.html:
CMHC and Health Canada sort mould by size, and the size decides who should clean it up:

SizeWhat countsWho should clean it
SmallOne to three patches, each smaller than 1 m²A healthy homeowner, with water and unscented dish detergent (CMHC)
MediumMore than three patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m² (32 square feet)Trained help; homeowners only with training and precautions
LargeA patch larger than 3 m², or many patches through the houseA qualified mould remediation contractor (CMHC)
  • Fix the moisture source first: a leak, poor drainage, or condensation from high humidity. Health Canada recommends 30–50% relative humidity.
  • For a small cleanup, wear safety glasses or goggles, an N95 mask if possible and household rubber gloves. People at risk from mould shouldn't clean it and should stay away.
  • Health Canada suggests professional help for extensive mould, especially growth that keeps coming back after cleaning.

sections.h2: Choosing a tester, lab or remediation contractor
sections.html:
Ask any St. John's tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause. For remediation, get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the area is cleaned.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: How much mould can I clean myself?
faq.a: CMHC says a healthy homeowner can clean one to three patches, each under 1 m², with water and unscented dish detergent. Larger areas need trained help or a remediation contractor.

faq.q: When should I hire a mould remediation contractor?
faq.a: For a single patch over 3 m², many patches through the house, or mould that keeps coming back after cleaning (CMHC, Health Canada).

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.lede: About 26,700 St. John's houses (64%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in St. John's houses

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.

sections.h2: The rules in Newfoundland and Labrador
sections.html:
In Newfoundland and Labrador, only certified asbestos abatement contractors may remove asbestos, and removal needs written notice to the OHS Division and a disposal permit.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

sections.h2: Testing and labs

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

sections.h2: If it's positive: abatement and removal

In Newfoundland and Labrador: Only certified asbestos abatement contractors may remove asbestos; the owner or contractor must notify the OHS Division in writing before starting and get a disposal permit.

lead-paint-testing.h1: Lead paint testing in St. John's
lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in St. John's: at-risk homes, testing and safe abatement
lead-paint-testing.description: 22% of St. John's's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 22% of St. John's's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 42% built from 1961 to 1990.

sections.h2: Which St. John's homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of St. John's's 42,120 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 22% were built before 1961 and 64% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

sections.h2: How to test
sections.html:
• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

sections.h2: If it's positive: lead paint abatement
sections.html:
Health Canada says leaving lead-based paint alone is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach, and covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling adds protection. Paint that's chipping, flaking or within reach of children is a serious hazard and has to come off carefully; consider hiring an expert before you start.

No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. must include lead in pre-renovation and demolition hazard inspections, and in Yukon before demolition. If you do the work yourself, Health Canada's precautions are:

  • Don't use sanders, heat guns or blowlamps: they create toxic dust and fumes. For do-it-yourself work, Health Canada suggests a chemical paint-stripper paste applied with a brush.
  • Move furniture out or cover it with plastic, seal doorways and vents with plastic sheeting and tape, and run a fan blowing out through an open window.
  • Wear goggles, gloves and a good-quality mask, work in 10-minute stretches with breaks outdoors, and don't eat, drink or smoke in the work area.
  • Clean up daily: put scrapings in a sealed container marked Hazardous Waste, follow your municipality's disposal instructions, and wipe surfaces with a damp cloth you throw away.
  • Keep children and pregnant people away until the work is done; Health Canada says there is no known safe level of lead exposure.

faq.q: Does my St. John's house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

faq.q: Should I remove lead paint or cover it?
faq.a: Health Canada says leaving it alone or covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach. Never sand it or use a heat gun, and consider hiring an expert for removal.

sections.h2: Wells in St. John's
sections.html:
Most of St. John's is on municipal water, but the city's boundaries include rural fringe areas.

Local program: For the free provincial bacteria test, St. John's samples go to the NL Public Health Laboratory at the Miller Centre rather than a Government Service Centre. Details

sections.h2: How testing works in Newfoundland and Labrador
sections.html: Free bacteria testing: sterile bottles are at Government Service Centres and the NL Public Health Laboratory. Chemistry goes to an approved private lab for a fee.

sections.h2: What to test for
sections.html:
• Bacteria (total coliforms and E. coli): at least once a year, and after flooding, heavy rain or work on the well.
  • Nitrate, especially near farmland or septic systems.
  • Metals and naturally occurring contaminants such as arsenic, uranium or manganese when a well is new and every few years after, depending on local geology.

faq.q: Is well water testing free in Newfoundland and Labrador?
faq.a: Free bacteria testing: sterile bottles are at Government Service Centres and the NL Public Health Laboratory. Chemistry goes to an approved private lab for a fee.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?
faq.a: For bacteria, at least once a year and after flooding, heavy rain or well work; many health units recommend more often. Test chemistry when the well is new and every few years after.

faq.a: Most of St. John's is on municipal water, but the city's boundaries include rural fringe areas.
